summary: Explains how to use the BGP-4 multiprotocol extensions, specifically the MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes, to convey IPv6 routing information between domains.

plainLanguage.summary: The system that lets large networks exchange their route maps was designed for the older, shorter addresses. This document explains how to use it for the newer, longer IPv6 addresses, and when a route must name both a global address and a local one.

questions: how does bgp-4 carry ipv6 routes
how does bgp carry ipv6 routes
bgp ipv6 next hop link-local address
subtitle: How BGP-4 carries IPv6 routes, and how to build the next hop field when link-local addresses are involved.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 was designed for IPv4, but IPv6 adds scoped unicast addresses, and link-local addresses do not fit the rules for the BGP-4 next hop attribute.
tldr.mechanism: Using the MP_REACH_NLRI attribute, a speaker puts the global IPv6 next hop in the Network Address of Next Hop field, optionally followed by a link-local address when it shares a subnet with the peer.
tldr.outcome: BGP-4 conveys IPv6 reachability information with the same procedures as before, plus rules for handling address scope.

facts.label: Next hop length, global plus link-local

sections.title: BGP-4 Meets IPv6
sections.content:
BGP-4, and path vector routing protocols in general, are mostly independent of the particular address family in use. The multiprotocol extensions define two attributes, MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI, that announce and withdraw reachability information. This document defines how compliant systems should use them for IPv6.

Unless stated otherwise, the normal BGP-4 procedures apply. The most significant difference from IPv4 is that IPv6 introduces scoped unicast addresses and defines when a particular address scope must be used, so the document concerns itself essentially with those scope rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The route-sharing protocol does not depend much on the kind of address it carries. Only a few rules about where an address is valid need to be added.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Scopes
sections.content:
IPv6 defines three unicast address scopes: global, site-local and link-local. Site-local addresses are valid only within a site and cannot be exported beyond it. This document does not distinguish global from site-local addresses and refers to both as global or non-link-local. Administrators must still respect scope restrictions, and the notions of a BGP-4 routing domain and a site are orthogonal.

Other IPv6 specifications say only link-local addresses can be used when generating ICMP Redirect messages and as next hop addresses in some routing protocols such as RIPng. So an IPv6 router must have a link-local next hop address for every directly connected route. Link-local addresses do not suit the rules for the BGP-4 next hop attribute, so a next hop sometimes has to carry both a global and a link-local address.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IPv6 addresses work anywhere and some work only on the local link. Some routes therefore need to name both kinds of address so the receiver knows which one to use.

sections.title: Building the Next Hop Field
sections.content:
A BGP speaker advertises in the Network Address of Next Hop field the global IPv6 address of the next hop, potentially followed by the link-local IPv6 address of the next hop. The Length of Next Hop Network Address field is set to 16 when only a global address is present, or 32 when a link-local address is included too.

The link-local address is included if and only if the speaker shares a common subnet with the entity identified by the global address and with the peer the route is being advertised to. In all other cases only the global address is sent, with length 16. As a result, a speaker advertising to an internal peer may remove the link-local address.
sections.plainLanguage: The speaker sends the global address of the next hop. It adds the link-local address only when it shares a local network segment with both the next hop and the peer. A length of 16 means a global address alone, and 32 means both are present.

sections.title: Transport and Security
sections.content:
The TCP connections that carry BGP-4 messages can be established over IPv4 or IPv6. BGP-4 derives implicit configuration from the address used to establish the session, so using TCP over IPv4 as the transport for IPv6 reachability information requires additional explicit configuration of the peer's network address. Using TCP over IPv6 also has the advantage of providing explicit confirmation of IPv6 reachability between the peers.

The BGP Identifier is distinct from that. It is a 32-bit unsigned integer exchanged in the OPEN message, must be unique in the network, and should be derived from an IPv4 address regardless of which addresses the session carries. The security section says no new security issues are raised beyond those already in BGP-4.
sections.plainLanguage: The two routers can exchange BGP over the old or the new address type. Running the session over IPv6 also proves that IPv6 works between them. The document adds no new security concerns beyond those BGP-4 already has.
